Phenylketonuria (PKU) is an autosomal recessive inborn error of phenylalanine metabolism caused by deficiency in the enzyme phenylalanine hydroxylase that converts phenylalanine into tyrosine. PKU management differs widely across Europe and therefore these guidelines have been developed aiming to optimize and standardize PKU care. Professionals from 10 different European countries developed the guidelines according to the AGREE (Appraisal of Guidelines for Research and Evaluation) method. Literature search, critical appraisal and evidence grading were conducted according to the SIGN (Scottish Intercollegiate Guidelines Network) method. The Delphi-method was used when there was no or little evidence available. External consultants reviewed the guidelines. Using these methods 70 statements were formulated based on the highest quality evidence available. The level of evidence of most recommendations is C or D. Although study designs and patient numbers are sub-optimal, many statements are convincing, important and relevant. Journal/Date: Frontiers in psychiatry (2019)

--- ABSTRACT ---
Phenylketonuria (PKU) is a recessive disorder of phenylalanine metabolism due to mutations in the gene for phenylalanine hydroxylase (PAH). Reduced PAH activity results in significant hyperphenylalaninemia, which leads to alterations in cerebral myelin and protein synthesis, as well as reduced levels of serotonin, dopamine, and noradrenaline in the brain. When untreated, brain development is grossly disrupted and significant intellectual impairment and behavioral disturbance occur. The advent of neonatal heel prick screening has allowed for diagnosis at birth, and the institution of a phenylalanine restricted diet. Dietary treatment, particularly when maintained across neurodevelopment and well into adulthood, has resulted in markedly improved outcomes at a cognitive and psychiatric level for individuals with PKU. However, few individuals can maintain full dietary control lifelong, and even with good control, an elevated risk remains of-in particular-mood, anxiety, and attentional disorders across the lifespan. Increasingly, dietary recommendations focus on maintaining continuous dietary treatment lifelong to optimize psychiatric and cognitive outcomes, although the effect of long-term protein restricted diets on brain function remains unknown. While psychiatric illness is very common in adult PKU populations, very little data exist to guide clinicians on optimal treatment. The advent of new treatments that do not require restrictive dietary management, such as the enzyme therapy Pegvaliase, holds the promise of allowing patients a relatively normal diet alongside optimized mental health and cognitive functioning.

key_findings.finding: An unrestricted vegetarian diet without phenylalanine-free medical formula is not an adequate metabolic treatment for classical PKU. Standard care is lifelong restriction of natural protein/phenylalanine plus phenylalanine-free amino-acid/protein substitute and low-protein foods; vegetarian status alone does not remove phenylalanine, because legumes, grains, nuts, seeds, dairy/eggs if included, and many plant-protein foods contribute Phe. The evidence retrieved supports formula as a cornerstone, while an unrestricted diet without medical food is described only in the context of effective phenylalanine-lowering therapy such as pegvaliase—not diet alone. A diagnosis Phe around 19 mg/dL (≈1140 µmol/L) is markedly above treatment targets and is compatible with classical/severe PKU, requiring urgent metabolic-specialist management.

source_tools.relevance: PKU guideline: untreated high Phe causes severe neurologic/behavioral disease; standard dietary treatment and lifelong control
PKU nutrition literature: lifelong protein restriction is complemented by Phe-free medical formulas; unrestricted diet without medical food is specifically linked to pegvaliase therapy
PKU dietary guideline search: treatment is based on protein restriction plus Phe-free medical formulas/protein substitutes
Disease ontology identifies classic PKU as a severe untreated form of PKU

key_findings.finding: At persistently elevated Phe in adolescence, the best-supported neuropsychiatric risks are executive-function impairment, inattention/sustained-attention deficits, slower processing, working-memory/inhibitory-control problems, hyperactivity/ADHD-like symptoms, emotional or behavioral dysregulation, anxiety, and depression/mood disorders. These problems can occur even in early-treated patients with less severe elevations, so a 15-year-old untreated at approximately 19 mg/dL is at particularly high risk; they should not be dismissed as ordinary adolescent behavior.

source_tools.relevance: PKU review: elevated Phe alters myelin/protein synthesis and monoamine neurotransmitters; untreated disease causes intellectual and behavioral disturbance, while treated cohorts still show mood, anxiety, and attentional disorders
Observational PKU study: mood disorders, anxiety/depression, hyperactivity/inattention, and executive-function deficits are recognized manifestations
Sapropterin randomized study: ADHD-inattentive symptoms and executive deficits were present and improved when Phe-lowering treatment was effective

key_findings.finding: Cognitive decline is a credible concern with prolonged poor metabolic control, especially reduced executive function, processing speed, sustained attention, memory, and fine-motor control. Untreated classical PKU can cause severe intellectual disability; in a late-diagnosed adolescent, the likely concern is worsening or failure to develop these functions rather than assuming inevitable global decline. Existing impairment may improve after Phe reduction, but recovery is variable and cannot be guaranteed, particularly after long-standing untreated exposure.

Review/search result: poor control and elevated Phe are associated with cognitive decline and adverse executive, processing-speed, attention, memory, and fine-motor outcomes
Treatment-response trial: attention and executive symptoms improved within weeks in Phe-responsive individuals

key_findings.finding: White-matter injury/dysmyelination is biologically and radiologically plausible in this setting. PKU is associated with altered cerebral myelin and MRI white-matter abnormalities; abnormalities are more frequent after adolescents stop treatment and can improve after Phe control is restored. Recent studies also report reversible white-matter changes after high-Phe exposure, but persistent or incomplete recovery remains possible, so MRI is clinically indicated only when neurologic/cognitive findings warrant it and should not substitute for immediate biochemical treatment.

source_tools.relevance: PKU review: untreated hyperphenylalaninemia alters cerebral myelin
Adolescent PKU neuroradiology report: white-matter abnormalities associated with stopping diet improved after treatment resumed, supporting Phe-related reversibility

key_findings.finding: Growth and skeletal consequences are important but less specific than the neuropsychiatric evidence. PKU patients with poor adherence can have reduced bone mineral density; adolescence is a critical period for peak bone accrual. An unrestricted vegetarian diet without formula also risks inadequate total protein, tyrosine, calcium, vitamin D, B12, iron, zinc, and other nutrients, potentially worsening growth, body composition, and bone health. The literature retrieved does not establish that elevated Phe alone invariably causes growth failure or bone disease, so these should be assessed rather than presumed.

key_findings.finding: Reversibility is partial and domain-specific: Phe reduction can improve attention, executive symptoms, psychiatric functioning, and Phe-related white-matter abnormalities, sometimes within weeks to months, but late treatment cannot be assumed to normalize IQ, established neurodevelopmental injury, or all mood/behavioral symptoms. A 15-year-old with Phe ~19 mg/dL should therefore be treated urgently rather than trialing an unrestricted vegetarian diet; evaluation should include serial Phe, nutritional status/growth, neuropsychological testing, psychiatric screening, and bone-health assessment, with treatment directed by a PKU metabolic team.

observations: Classical PKU requires lifelong restriction of natural phenylalanine/protein plus phenylalanine-free medical protein substitute; an unrestricted vegetarian diet alone does not maintain metabolic control.

Persistent high phenylalanine in adolescence is associated with executive-function impairment, inattention, slower processing, working-memory and inhibitory-control problems, hyperactivity, and mood or behavioral dysregulation.
Cognitive and white-matter abnormalities may improve after phenylalanine reduction, but recovery is variable and incomplete.
